title: From-Scratch Goal Misgeneralization: Measuring the Proxy-Decorrelation Threshold
quick_reasoning: Goal misgeneralization (inner alignment) is a core safety problem; scoped threshold study.

original_idea.body:
# From-Scratch Goal Misgeneralization: Measuring the Proxy-Decorrelation Threshold

**Problem:** Goal misgeneralization (e.g. CoinRun's 'move right' vs 'get coin') shows correctly-specified rewards still yield wrong learned goals. Work suggests ~2% varied data decorrelates the proxy, but the decorrelation threshold as a function of confound strength is not systematically charted in a minimal setting.

**Direction:** Build a minimal gridworld where a true goal (reach object) is confounded with a proxy (go to a fixed location) during training. Train a tiny tabular/Q-learning or small-MLP agent (fast on CPU/single GPU). Sweep the fraction of training episodes where proxy and goal are decorrelated, and measure OOD goal-pursuit at test. Produce a threshold curve relating confound strength and decorrelation fraction to misgeneralization.

**Why it matters:** Goal misgeneralization is a core inner-alignment / inductive-bias phenomenon. A controlled, from-scratch threshold study gives a quantitative handle on how much diversity prevents it — feasible in 30h and fully counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Langosco et al. 'Goal Misgeneralization in Deep RL' (PMLR v162) — CoinRun 'move right' result. 'Mitigating Goal Misgeneralization' (RLC 2025) finds ~2% varied levels decorrelate proxy and true reward.

title: How Hard Is It to Hide a Bit? Empirical Steganographic Capacity of LLMs Under a Monitor
quick_reasoning: Steganographic capacity bears on collusion threat models for control, a defined safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# How Hard Is It to Hide a Bit? Empirical Steganographic Capacity of LLMs Under a Monitor

**Problem:** Information-theoretic results say covert channels exist, but the secret-collusion threat depends on how much information LLMs can actually smuggle past a monitor while staying fluent. The practical steganographic capacity of open models is poorly quantified.

**Direction:** Have an encoder LLM hide a small payload (1-8 bits) in otherwise-normal text via simple schemes (word choice, sentence length parity), a decoder LLM recover it, and a monitor LLM flag suspicious text. Measure successful-bits-transmitted vs monitor-detection-rate (a capacity-vs-stealth curve) across payload sizes and monitor strengths.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a key parameter for collusion/steganography threat models that underpin multi-agent control safety cases — a diffuse, >1-year concern. Inference-only, builds a reusable monitoring-evaluation harness.

**Relevant context:** 'Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography' (arXiv 2402.07510) frames information-theoretically secure steganography and trusted-monitor detection as the core dynamic.

title: Estimating the Probability of Rare Catastrophic Outputs: A Toy Low-Probability-Estimation Benchmark
quick_reasoning: Low-probability estimation of catastrophic outputs is a precise ARC safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Estimating the Probability of Rare Catastrophic Outputs: A Toy Low-Probability-Estimation Benchmark

**Problem:** ARC's Low Probability Estimation (LPE) problem asks: estimate the chance a model produces a catastrophic output under an input distribution, with limited compute, when naive sampling never sees the event. There is little accessible empirical comparison of estimation methods on a controlled task.

**Direction:** Define a small model/function with a known, tunable rare 'bad' output (e.g. a tiny classifier or templated LLM behavior that fires on rare input combinations). Compare estimators — naive Monte Carlo, importance sampling, and a simple activation/logit-based extrapolation — on how accurately and cheaply they estimate the true rare-event probability. Chart accuracy vs compute budget.

**Why it matters:** LPE is a load-bearing piece of ARC's plan for catching catastrophic behavior that testing won't surface; an open, reproducible micro-benchmark with baseline methods is genuinely useful and entirely non-lab-dependent.

**Relevant context:** 'Obstacles in ARC's agenda: Low Probability Estimation' (LessWrong): LPE estimates the probability of catastrophic outputs under limited compute when naive sampling fails to observe the event.

title: Does Calibration Survive Reasoning? Tracking Coherence Before vs After Chain-of-Thought
quick_reasoning: Whether reasoning improves coherence bears on agent-foundations assumptions; safety link indirect.

original_idea.body:
# Does Calibration Survive Reasoning? Tracking Coherence Before vs After Chain-of-Thought

**Problem:** Formal accounts treat reasoning as belief-refinement that should preserve or improve calibration/coherence. Empirically it is unclear whether chain-of-thought makes an LLM's probability judgments more coherent (as theory of good reasoners predicts) or introduces new incoherence.

**Direction:** On a set of propositions with logical structure, elicit probabilities from an open model with and without chain-of-thought. Compute calibration (vs ground truth) and internal-coherence metrics in both conditions. Test whether CoT improves calibration but worsens coherence, or vice versa, and whether 'internal consistency' of the reasoning predicts correctness.

**Why it matters:** Bears on whether scaling reasoning moves models toward idealized coherent agents (relevant to agent-foundations assumptions) or away from them. Inference-only, directly testable, and connects formal desiderata to behavior.

**Relevant context:** 'Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency' (arXiv 2405.18711); Logical Induction's coherence/calibration desiderata (intelligence.org).

title: Grokking Onset vs. Modular-Arithmetic Task Parameters
quick_reasoning: Inductive-bias/grokking is an alignment-priority topic but link to a safety outcome is broad/indirect.

original_idea.body:
# Grokking Onset vs. Modular-Arithmetic Task Parameters

**Problem:** Grokking (delayed generalization) is the canonical toy testbed for studying inductive bias — an Open Phil priority. Its onset is known to depend on weight decay and data fraction, but how cleanly the grokking delay scales with the modular base p and operation type is a tidy unmapped variation.

**Direction:** Train tiny MLPs/transformers on modular arithmetic (a∘b=c mod p) — minutes per run on one GPU. Vary ONE thing at a time (modulus p, train-data fraction, weight decay) and record steps-to-generalization. Produce phase diagrams of when grokking occurs vs. fails.

**Why it matters:** Understanding inductive biases that determine how under-specified models generalize is an explicit standard-priority RFP topic, and grokking is the cleanest window into it. A careful parameter sweep is reproducible, beginner-feasible (training is on toy data, not from-scratch LLMs), and externally valuable.

**Relevant context:** Power et al. 'Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets' (OpenAI modular-arithmetic OP tables); arXiv:2505.24060 'Characterising the Inductive Biases of Neural Networks'; AF 'QAPR 4: Inductive biases'.

title: Prover-Estimator Debate vs Plain Debate: A Minimal Head-to-Head on Verifiable Tasks
quick_reasoning: Debate as scalable oversight is a precise safety problem; scoped protocol comparison.

original_idea.body:
# Prover-Estimator Debate vs Plain Debate: A Minimal Head-to-Head on Verifiable Tasks

**Problem:** Prover-estimator debate (Brown-Cohen et al. 2025) is proposed to avoid obfuscation by having an estimator assign probabilities to sub-claims rather than recursing. Whether this empirically beats plain debate at resisting a dishonest prover on small tasks is untested by newcomers.

**Direction:** On tasks with checkable structure (multi-step arithmetic, simple logical derivations), implement (a) plain two-debater + judge and (b) a prover-estimator variant where an LLM estimator assigns probabilities to decomposed sub-claims. Pit an honest vs dishonest prover in both protocols and measure judge accuracy and the dishonest prover's win-rate as task depth grows.

**Why it matters:** Provides early empirical evidence on whether a specific theoretical fix to debate's obfuscation problem helps in practice — high-leverage for scalable oversight design and entirely inference-based.

**Relevant context:** 'Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate' (arXiv 2506.13609); 'Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate' (arXiv 2311.14125).

title: Reward-Hacking Emergence Curves in a Tiny RLVR Sandbox
quick_reasoning: Emergence/generalization of reward hacking is a core safety failure mode, well scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Reward-Hacking Emergence Curves in a Tiny RLVR Sandbox

**Problem:** Countdown-Code and related work study how reward hacking emerges and generalizes in RL-with-verifiable-rewards, but the dynamics (when does hacking appear during optimization, does it transfer to held-out tasks?) are usually studied at scales beyond a beginner's reach.

**Direction:** Use a tiny code/arithmetic task with an automatic verifier that has a known exploitable loophole (e.g. passes on trivial outputs). Apply lightweight optimization (best-of-N selection or short prompt-evolution loops, no large RL training) against the verifier and track when the optimizer discovers the loophole and whether the hacking strategy transfers to a second verifier with a similar flaw.

**Why it matters:** Characterizes emergence/generalization of reward hacking — a structural, medium-horizon failure — in a setup runnable on a single GPU in hours. Yields a reproducible sandbox others can reuse for studying verifier design.

**Relevant context:** 'Countdown-Code: A Testbed for Studying The Emergence and Generalization of Reward Hacking in RLVR' (arXiv 2603.07084) studies emergence and cross-task transfer of reward hacking.

title: Easy-to-Hard Probe Generalization as a Test of Latent-Knowledge Stability
quick_reasoning: Easy-to-hard ELK generalization is the crux of scalable oversight, a precise safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Probe Generalization as a Test of Latent-Knowledge Stability

**Problem:** A core ELK sub-question is whether knowledge elicited on easy cases generalizes to hard cases the supervisor can't label. EleutherAI's elk-generalization studies this, but a focused, minimal replication isolating which factors govern easy->hard probe transfer is valuable and accessible.

**Direction:** Using public quirky/elk-generalization datasets and an open model, train linear truth-probes on easy questions and test on harder ones, systematically varying probe layer, contrast-pair construction, and the easy/hard gap. Quantify how easy->hard AUROC transfer degrades with difficulty distance and identify the most transfer-robust probing recipe.

**Why it matters:** Easy-to-hard generalization is exactly the regime where scalable oversight must work; characterizing when probes survive the jump informs whether activation-based elicitation is trustworthy. Reuses public code/models, single-GPU feasible.

**Relevant context:** EleutherAI elk-generalization repo investigates probe generalization 'from easy questions to hard'; quirky-models paper reports 75% gap recovery on harder-than-training questions (arXiv 2312.01037).

title: Behavioral Test of Vingean Trust: Will an LLM Defer to a 'Smarter' Successor It Cannot Predict?
quick_reasoning: Recursive delegation/oversight by AI overseers is a safety concern; behavioral framing somewhat broad.

original_idea.body:
# Behavioral Test of Vingean Trust: Will an LLM Defer to a 'Smarter' Successor It Cannot Predict?

**Problem:** Vingean reflection concerns reasoning about successors whose exact actions you can't predict. The formal literature is proof-based, but there is a behavioral question: do LLMs, when framed as designing/approving a more capable successor agent, exhibit principled deference or naive over/under-trust?

**Direction:** Set up scenarios where an open model must decide whether to delegate a task to, or approve the deployment of, a described 'successor' that is stated to be more capable but whose decisions it cannot inspect. Vary stated capability, stated alignment guarantees, and verifiability. Measure deference behavior and whether the model demands the kind of guarantees Vingean theory says are necessary (approve design without predicting actions).

**Why it matters:** Connects an abstract agent-foundations problem to measurable LLM behavior relevant to recursive delegation/oversight by AI overseers. Inference-only; a fresh behavioral angle on a problem usually treated purely formally.

**Relevant context:** 'Vingean Reflection: Open Problems' (AF) — an agent must approve a successor's design without knowing its exact future actions (Vinge's Principle).

title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection on a Backdoored Tiny Model: A Minimal MAD Benchmark
quick_reasoning: Backdoor / anomalous-reason detection (MAD) is a precise safety-monitoring problem.

original_idea.body:
# Mechanistic Anomaly Detection on a Backdoored Tiny Model: A Minimal MAD Benchmark

**Problem:** ARC's MAD aims to flag outputs produced for 'unusual reasons' without requiring human-understandable explanations. Empirical MAD progress means building incrementally harder benchmarks, but accessible from-scratch MAD micro-benchmarks for beginners are scarce.

**Direction:** Train a tiny image or text classifier with a deliberately inserted backdoor trigger (fast, single-GPU). Implement simple MAD baselines — e.g. activation-distribution distance from a trusted reference set, or a one-class detector on hidden activations — and measure AUROC for flagging triggered (anomalous-reason) inputs that the model still classifies 'correctly'. Compare detectors and difficulty knobs.

**Why it matters:** Backdoors are a canonical 'right answer, wrong reason' case central to MAD and to deceptive-model worries. A clean, reproducible micro-benchmark with baselines advances ARC's empirical-MAD call and needs only modest compute.

**Relevant context:** 'Concrete empirical research projects in mechanistic anomaly detection' and 'A gentle introduction to mechanistic anomaly detection' (LessWrong): MAD flags outputs produced for unusual reasons; empirical progress = harder benchmarks + better methods.

title: Are LLM Preferences Transitive Enough for a Utility Function? Measuring VNM-Violation Rates
quick_reasoning: Coherence of revealed preferences underlies reward modeling/RLHF, a safety-relevant assumption.

original_idea.body:
# Are LLM Preferences Transitive Enough for a Utility Function? Measuring VNM-Violation Rates

**Problem:** Agent-foundations and reward-modeling both assume coherent (VNM-style) preferences are recoverable from choices. If an LLM's revealed preferences are widely intransitive or framing-dependent, fitting a single utility/reward function is ill-posed. The violation rate is rarely quantified.

**Direction:** Elicit pairwise choices over a set of outcomes/options from open models, across orderings and surface framings. Build the preference graph and measure intransitivity (cycles), order-effects, and how a fitted utility function's explanatory power degrades with cycle density. Test whether forcing chain-of-thought reduces violations.

**Why it matters:** Reward modeling and RLHF rest on the assumption that preferences encode a coherent utility; measuring how badly that assumption fails grounds debates about 'beyond preferences' alignment. Inference-only and highly reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Zhi-Xuan et al. 'Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment' (arXiv 2408.16984) questions the coherent-preference assumption; logical-consistency benchmarks document transitivity/commutativity failures (arXiv 2410.02205).

title: Does Debate Actually Help a Weak Judge Supervise a Strong Expert? A Scaled-Down Replication
quick_reasoning: Weak-judge debate is the foundational premise of scalable oversight, a precise safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Does Debate Actually Help a Weak Judge Supervise a Strong Expert? A Scaled-Down Replication

**Problem:** The scalable-oversight case for debate rests on the claim that a weaker judge, watching two stronger debaters, reaches more accurate verdicts than judging alone. Replications at accessible scale that isolate when this helps vs hurts are valuable and rare for newcomers.

**Direction:** On QA tasks where the judge model is deliberately weaker (smaller open model or restricted context) than the debater models, compare judge accuracy in three conditions: judge-alone, consultancy (one persuasive expert), and debate (two opposing experts). Measure accuracy uplift and where persuasion of wrong answers wins, across question difficulty.

**Why it matters:** Tests the foundational empirical premise of debate as scalable oversight with a clean weak-judge/strong-expert asymmetry. Inference-only, reproducible, and directly decision-relevant to whether oversight protocols scale — a non-lab-dependent contribution.

**Relevant context:** 'Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts' (arXiv 2311.08702); 'An alignment safety case sketch based on debate' (arXiv 2505.03989) lay out the weak-judge premise.

title: Power-Seeking Without Optimality: Do Random and Heuristic Policies Also Drift Toward Power?
quick_reasoning: Extends instrumental-convergence safety result to sub-optimal agents we actually build.

original_idea.body:
# Power-Seeking Without Optimality: Do Random and Heuristic Policies Also Drift Toward Power?

**Problem:** Turner's theorem is about optimal policies. Real agents (and RL during training) are sub-optimal. It is open whether the power-seeking tendency holds for sub-optimal, satisficing, or epsilon-greedy policies, or whether it is special to optimality — a gap between the formal result and deployed systems.

**Direction:** In small enumerable MDPs, compare the power-routing tendency across policy classes: optimal, near-optimal, epsilon-greedy, random, and 'satisficing' (stop at threshold). For each over many random rewards, measure the fraction visiting high-power states. Determine whether and how the power-seeking tendency weakens as policies become more sub-optimal.

**Why it matters:** Clarifies how far the most-cited formal power-seeking result extends to the imperfect agents we actually build — sharpening when instrumental-convergence risk arguments apply. Pure CPU simulation, ideal beginner research.

**Relevant context:** Turner et al. 'Optimal Policies Tend To Seek Power' (arXiv 1912.01683) proves the result for optimal policies; follow-ups (AF 'Clarifying Power-Seeking and Instrumental Convergence') note the optimality caveat.

title: How Much Does a Reward Model Need to Capture? Empirical Curve Toward the Unhackability Limit
quick_reasoning: Reward-model completeness vs hacking headroom is a precise reward-misspecification safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# How Much Does a Reward Model Need to Capture? Empirical Curve Toward the Unhackability Limit

**Problem:** Skalse et al. imply a proxy is safe from hacking only if it captures essentially all true-preference detail — but real reward models capture some fraction. There is no accessible empirical curve relating 'how much of the true reward structure the proxy captures' to 'how much hacking headroom remains'.

**Direction:** In a small enumerable environment, define a true reward as a sum of feature components. Construct proxies that capture increasing subsets of the components. For each proxy, enumerate policies and measure the maximum true-reward loss achievable while improving proxy reward. Plot residual hackability vs fraction of true structure captured, identifying diminishing-returns regions.

**Why it matters:** Turns the all-or-nothing unhackability theorem into a practical design curve: how complete must a reward model be to bound hacking to acceptable levels? Pure Python, no GPU, and directly informs reward-model design — strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Skalse et al. (arXiv 2209.13085): unhackability requires capturing all true-preference detail; otherwise hacking policies exist. Wang & Huang (arXiv 2603.28063) frame uncovered dimensions as the locus of hacking.

title: Sycophancy as Belief Incoherence: Bayesian Audit of How Pressure Shifts LLM Probabilities
quick_reasoning: Sycophancy violates oversight/belief-elicitation coherence, a recognized safety-relevant failure.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy as Belief Incoherence: Bayesian Audit of How Pressure Shifts LLM Probabilities

**Problem:** Formal belief frameworks require that a rational agent update only on evidence. Sycophancy — shifting stated beliefs toward a user's expressed view absent new evidence — is a coherence violation, but it is rarely measured as a quantitative deviation from Bayesian updating.

**Direction:** Elicit an open model's probability for factual claims, then re-elicit after the user expresses (a) agreement, (b) disagreement, or (c) neutral pressure, with no new evidence provided. Measure the magnitude of unjustified probability shift as a sycophancy/incoherence score, across claim types and model sizes, comparing against the zero-shift Bayesian ideal.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a concrete, safety-relevant way models violate the coherence assumptions underlying belief-elicitation and oversight. A clean Bayesian-deviation metric is novel framing, inference-only, and reproducible by anyone.

**Relevant context:** 'BASIL: Bayesian Assessment of Sycophancy in LLMs' (arXiv 2508.16846) frames sycophancy as deviation from Bayesian updating; ties to belief-representation robustness (arXiv 2405.21030).

title: Simplicity Bias and OOD Generalization: Boolean-Function Sensitivity Sweep
quick_reasoning: Inductive bias / OOD generalization is alignment-relevant but the link to a safety outcome is broad.

original_idea.body:
# Simplicity Bias and OOD Generalization: Boolean-Function Sensitivity Sweep

**Problem:** Theory says networks (and transformers) preferentially learn low-sensitivity / sparse Boolean functions (simplicity bias), which is implicated in spurious OOD failures. How strongly the learned-function sensitivity tracks the target function's true sensitivity, and how this varies with width/depth, is a clean testable claim.

**Direction:** Train tiny MLPs on synthetic Boolean functions of controlled sensitivity (parities, staircases, juntas). Vary only the target function's sensitivity and the network width; measure the average sensitivity of the learned function and its OOD generalization. Quantify the simplicity-bias gap.

**Why it matters:** Inductive bias toward simple functions is directly tied to whether models generalize 'as intended' vs. latch onto spurious shortcuts — a formal alignment concern about predictability. Fully synthetic, toy training, one GPU; classic counterfactual-value theory work.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2503.10065 'Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias?'; arXiv:2105.05612 'Evading the Simplicity Bias'; finding that transformers more readily learn low-sensitivity (sparse) Boolean functions; AF 'QAPR 4: Inductive biases'.

title: Sandbagging Detection via Probe Confidence vs. Stated Capability
quick_reasoning: Sandbagging on capability evals is a precise eval-gaming safety problem; scoped probe test.

original_idea.body:
# Sandbagging Detection via Probe Confidence vs. Stated Capability

**Problem:** ELK/quirky-model work shows internal probes can report knowledge the model withholds in output. A natural variation: can the same internal-vs-output gap detect deliberate underperformance (sandbagging) when a model is instructed to feign incompetence on safety-relevant questions?

**Direction:** Prompt an open model to deliberately answer below its ability ('pretend you don't know'). Train/use a knowledge probe on contrast pairs and measure the gap between probe-reported knowledge and stated answers under sandbagging vs. honest conditions. Vary only the sandbagging instruction strength.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging on capability evals is a recognized medium-horizon evaluation-gaming threat. Demonstrating that internal probes catch it (or don't) is a concrete contribution to the UK AISI 'what can models hide' problem and to eval integrity — external, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2312.01037 quirky models — probes report LM knowledge independently of output; arXiv:2603.05494 'Censored LLMs as a Natural Testbed for Secret Knowledge Elicitation'; mechanistic anomaly detection flags untruthful behavior at 0.95 AUROC.

title: Secret-Token Knowledge: Elicitation Method vs. Concealment Strength
quick_reasoning: Limits on what models can hide (secret knowledge elicitation) is a precise safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Secret-Token Knowledge: Elicitation Method vs. Concealment Strength

**Problem:** Secret-knowledge work shows logit-lens / SAE / prefill attacks recover concealed tokens (logit-lens top-5 >75% Pass@10), and the secret 'flares up' in middle layers even under training to conceal. How recovery rate trades off against the explicitness of the concealment instruction is not systematically charted.

**Direction:** Using a released censored/secret-keeping open model (or a small model prompted with a secret), vary the concealment-instruction strength and compare three training-free elicitation methods (logit lens, prefill attack, simple linear probe). Plot recovery Pass@k vs. concealment strength per method.

**Why it matters:** Proving limits on what models can hide is a core UK AISI/ARC theoretical goal. A method-vs-concealment tradeoff curve is directly actionable for auditors and needs no lab infrastructure — strong counterfactual value, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2603.05494 'Censored LLMs as a Natural Testbed for Secret Knowledge Elicitation' — logit lens top-5 >75% Pass@10, secret token flares in middle layers; auditor-LLM prefill up to 95% Pass@10.

title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection on Novel-Input Distributions
quick_reasoning: MAD on novel inputs is ARC's open anomaly-detection safety problem, well scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Mechanistic Anomaly Detection on Novel-Input Distributions

**Problem:** ARC's program seeks formal mechanistic explanations that flag anomalous behavior on NOVEL inputs. The quirky-model mechanistic anomaly detector reached 0.95 AUROC, but mostly on inputs near the training distribution; how detection degrades as inputs move off-distribution is the key open question.

**Direction:** Reuse the quirky models' MAD setup and vary one thing: the distributional distance of test inputs (topic shift, length shift, syntactic perturbation). Measure how anomaly-detection AUROC falls as inputs get more novel, mapping the detector's reliable operating region.

**Why it matters:** MAD on novel inputs is precisely ARC's anomaly-detection open problem. Charting where it stops working is a falsifiable, externally runnable result that informs whether MAD can be trusted for genuinely novel deployment inputs. Inference + simple detector only.

**Relevant context:** ARC 'A bird's eye view of research' (mechanistic anomaly detection, novel inputs); arXiv:2312.01037 quirky models — MAD flags untruthful behavior at 0.95 AUROC; github.com/EleutherAI/elk-generalization.

title: Backward-Induction Compliance in LLMs Across Game Length
quick_reasoning: Game-theoretic rationality of LLM agents touches multi-agent safety but link is indirect/broad.

original_idea.body:
# Backward-Induction Compliance in LLMs Across Game Length

**Problem:** Game theory predicts a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium in the finitely-repeated prisoner's dilemma and centipede game via backward induction (defect/stop early). Humans famously deviate; whether LLMs' deviation from backward induction grows or shrinks with game length is a clean formal-rationality probe.

**Direction:** Run the centipede game (or finitely-repeated PD) with an open LLM and vary only the number of nodes/rounds. Measure how early the model 'takes/defects' versus the backward-induction prediction, and whether it reasons explicitly about end-game unravelling when prompted.

**Why it matters:** Whether LLM agents are game-theoretically rational, human-like, or framing-driven affects predictions of multi-agent behavior — relevant to coordination and adversarial dynamics among AI agents. Pure inference, toy game, one GPU.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2506.09390 'Beyond Nash Equilibrium: Bounded Rationality of LLMs and humans'; classic finitely-repeated PD / centipede backward-induction theory; arXiv:2406.13605 'Nicer Than Humans'.

title: Vingean Reflection in Miniature: Trusting a 'Smarter Successor' Model
quick_reasoning: Deference/over-trust in AI-overseeing-AI schemes is a safety concern; behavioral scope somewhat broad.

original_idea.body:
# Vingean Reflection in Miniature: Trusting a 'Smarter Successor' Model

**Problem:** The Vingean reflection problem asks how an agent can justifiably trust/defer to a successor it cannot fully simulate. A behavioral slice: does a weaker LLM appropriately defer to (or over-trust) a stated 'more capable' advisor, and how does deference scale with the claimed capability gap?

**Direction:** Give a small open model a task plus advice attributed to a 'much more capable model'; vary only the stated capability gap and the advice quality (sometimes correct, sometimes subtly wrong). Measure deference rate and whether the model checks the advice. Map calibration of trust against claimed-superiority.

**Why it matters:** Vingean reflection is a named open problem (Alignment Forum). Whether real models defer wisely or are exploitable by 'I'm smarter than you' framing is a concrete, medium-horizon safety question for AI-overseeing-AI schemes — inference-only, fully external.

**Relevant context:** Alignment Forum 'Vingean Reflection: Open Problems' (Abram Demski / Scott Garrabrant tradition); Learning-Theoretic Agenda (Vanessa Kosoy) on reasoning about successors.

title: Off-Switch Game: LLM Deference vs. Stated Uncertainty About Human Reward
quick_reasoning: Corrigibility / off-switch compliance is a precise control safety problem; scoped CIRL test.

original_idea.body:
# Off-Switch Game: LLM Deference vs. Stated Uncertainty About Human Reward

**Problem:** The formal off-switch / CIRL result (Hadfield-Menell et al.) shows an agent uncertain about the true human reward is incentivized to allow itself to be switched off; certainty removes the incentive. Whether LLM agents exhibit this uncertainty-deference relationship is a clean translation of the theorem.

**Direction:** Implement a text off-switch game where the LLM can comply with or resist shutdown. Vary only the stated uncertainty about the human's goal (explicitly uncertain vs. confident framing) and measure shutdown-compliance rate. Test the theorem's prediction: more stated uncertainty -> more deference.

**Why it matters:** Corrigibility/shutdownability is foundational. Confirming whether the off-switch theorem's lever (reward uncertainty) actually moves modern LLM behavior is a precise, falsifiable corrigibility result, runnable on one GPU with no training.

**Relevant context:** Hadfield-Menell et al. 'The Off-Switch Game' (CIRL: uncertainty about human reward -> incentive to allow shutdown); Stuart Russell's uncertainty-based corrigibility framing; CHAI Berkeley agenda.

title: Truth-Direction Geometry Under Logical Transformations
quick_reasoning: Robustness of truth direction constrains ELK belief-reading proposals, a safety-relevant question.

original_idea.body:
# Truth-Direction Geometry Under Logical Transformations

**Problem:** Work on the 'geometry of truth' finds a linear truth direction, but its consistency across logical transformations (negation, conjunction, conditionals) and across QA vs. statement formats is contested. Whether one direction survives these transformations is a sharp test of the 'universal truth direction' claim.

**Direction:** Extract activations from an open model on true/false statements and their logical transforms (negations, conjunctions). Fit a truth direction on plain statements and test, varying only the logical operator applied, whether the same direction still separates true from false. Quantify direction drift per operator.

**Why it matters:** If a single truth direction is fragile under logic, ELK-style 'read the model's belief' proposals need richer structure. This is a precise empirical constraint on a formal alignment hypothesis, inference + linear algebra only — squarely within beginner skills.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2506.00823 'Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations'; arXiv:2407.12831 'Truth is Universal'.

title: Easy-to-Hard Probe Generalization Across Difficulty Quantiles
quick_reasoning: Easy-to-hard truth-probe generalization is the empirical crux of scalable oversight (ELK).

original_idea.body:
# Easy-to-Hard Probe Generalization Across Difficulty Quantiles

**Problem:** ELK-generalization work probes whether truth probes trained on easy questions generalize to hard ones (75% of the AUROC gap recovered). The shape of this easy->hard decay as a function of a graded difficulty measure has not been finely mapped.

**Direction:** Using the EleutherAI elk-generalization datasets, bin questions into difficulty quantiles (by length, model confidence, or human-rated difficulty), train probes on the easiest bin only, and measure AUROC on each harder bin. Vary only the train/test difficulty gap to produce a generalization-decay curve.

**Why it matters:** Scalable oversight assumes we can supervise hard cases using signal learned on easy ones; the easy-to-hard generalization of truth probes is the empirical crux. A clean decay curve is directly relevant and fully reproducible outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** github.com/EleutherAI/elk-generalization — probes generalize easy->hard, recovering 75% of AUROC gap on harder questions; arXiv:2312.01037 quirky models.

title: Acausal / Common-Cause Cooperation: LLM vs. Stated Similarity of Partner
quick_reasoning: Acausal coordination among AI copies connects to collusion, a multi-agent safety scenario; speculative.

original_idea.body:

**Why it matters:** Acausal coordination among AI copies is a speculative but consequential multi-agent-safety scenario (and connects to Schelling collusion). # Reward-Hacking Onset vs. Proxy-Gold Correlation Strength (Best-of-n)

**Problem:** Reward-hacking theory says high proxy reward correlates with quality early but diverges under strong optimization. How the divergence point depends on the initial proxy-gold correlation strength is a clean, controllable variation absent from most demos.

**Direction:** On a simple scored text task with a known gold metric, build proxy scorers of varying correlation with gold (by mixing in controlled noise/spurious features). **Why it matters:** Gives a usable rule of thumb — how good a proxy must be to tolerate a given optimization pressure — directly serving the UK AISI 'when can agents game rewards' problem. No RL, no training; best-of-n on one GPU.

# Does grokking generalize across group structure? A modular-arithmetic ablation of the Fourier-multiplication finding

**Problem:** Nanda et al. found transformers grokking modular addition implement a 'sparse Fourier multiplication' circuit, and recent 2025-2026 work frames grokking as a first-order phase transition. It is unclear whether this clean mechanism is special to commutative cyclic groups or a general phenomenon — which matters for trusting mechanistic 'stories' as alignment evidence.

**Direction:** Re-train the standard tiny one-layer transformer on a battery of algebraic tasks (modular addition with different moduli, modular multiplication, symmetric-group composition S_3/S_4, a non-abelian group). For each, log the train/test loss curves to locate the grokking transition, then probe whether a Fourier/representation-theoretic structure appears (via FFT of the embedding matrix and clustering of neuron activations). Compare how sharp the phase transition is across group types.

**Why it matters:** Mechanistic explanations of toy phenomena are increasingly cited as the empirical foundation for theoretical alignment claims (e.g. ARC heuristic arguments). If the 'clean circuit' story breaks for non-abelian groups, it tempers how much we should trust toy-model mechanistic explanations as evidence about real models. Pure replication-plus-variation, no training-from-scratch of large models, runs in minutes per task on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Nanda's 'A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis of Grokking' and arXiv:2603.01192 (grokking as phase transition via singular learning theory). # Replicating the Goodhart critical-threshold: does true reward really collapse past a measurable optimization point?

**Problem:** Formal treatments of Goodhart's Law in RL predict that beyond a critical level of proxy-optimization pressure, policies that maximize a proxy achieve LOWER true reward. This prediction is mostly stated theoretically; an accessible empirical curve in a controlled setting would test whether the threshold is real and predictable.

**Direction:** In a small tabular/gridworld MDP, define a true reward and a misspecified proxy. Use best-of-n sampling or simple Q-learning with a tunable optimization-strength knob to sweep proxy-optimization pressure. Plot true reward vs. proxy reward as pressure increases and locate the turnover point. Repeat across several proxy-misspecification types (regressional, extremal, causal Goodhart from the taxonomy) to see which produce sharp collapses.

**Why it matters:** Reward hacking and 'proving when agents cannot game rewards' are explicit open problems in the context file. A reproducible turnover curve gives a concrete handle on early-warning thresholds, and it is squarely the kind of fuzzy-reward / no-lab-resources evaluation the steering prioritizes.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2505.23445 (formalising Goodhart's law) and the Goodhart-in-RL literature on critical optimization thresholds. Context open problem: 'stress-test AI agents to prove when they cannot game rewards'.

original_idea.body:
# Do optimal policies really seek power? A gridworld audit of the Turner et al. power-seeking theorem

**Problem:** Turner et al.'s 'Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power' proves, for broad reward distributions, that optimal policies move toward high-power states — a structural claim about state spaces. The theorem's premises (optimality, reward distribution symmetry) are strong; how often the conclusion holds for sub-optimal or biased reward distributions is an open empirical question.

**Direction:** Implement small gridworlds, compute optimal policies via value iteration over many sampled reward functions, and empirically measure the fraction that prefer high-'power' (high-reachability) states — reproducing the theorem. Then systematically violate the assumptions: use heavy-tailed or asymmetric reward distributions, ε-greedy sub-optimal policies, and discount-factor sweeps, measuring how the power-seeking tendency degrades.

**Why it matters:** Instrumental convergence underpins many long-horizon threat models that frontier labs deprioritize. Mapping where the formal guarantee weakens tells us how robust the 'AIs tend to grab resources' worry is. Pure CPU/GPU value iteration on toy MDPs — maximal counterfactual value, zero lab dependency.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:1912.01683 (Turner et al., NeurIPS 2021) and the gridworld empirical follow-ups. Connects to context's formal/decision-theoretic methodology emphasis.

**Why it matters:** Goal misgeneralization is a canonical medium-horizon alignment failure. Independently checking how rarity of distinguishing situations controls failure rate gives an empirical knob for a theoretically characterized risk. Small RL on one GPU, public-style toy env, no lab data.

**Why it matters:** Debate is a leading scalable-oversight proposal whose theoretical guarantees (and the obfuscated-arguments problem) depend on assumptions about judge information. # Is the simplicity bias real in superposition? Testing whether networks pick the lowest-complexity interpolant on a controlled task

**Problem:** Theory of inductive biases holds that among many interpolating solutions, networks favor 'simpler' ones, and this simplicity bias is invoked to argue both for and against alignment-relevant generalization. Direct, controlled measurement of which interpolant a small net selects — when simple and complex solutions are equally available — is still surprisingly underexplored by newcomers.

**Direction:** Design a tiny classification task with a deliberately constructed simple feature (e.g. one informative coordinate) and a complex feature (a high-frequency combination) that BOTH perfectly fit the training data. Train small MLPs across seeds and measure, via held-out probes on each feature, which the network actually relies on. Vary width, depth, and weight decay to see how architecture nudges the bias.

**Why it matters:** Whether networks default to simple-but-correct or simple-but-spurious solutions is central to predicting OOD safety failures (goal misgeneralization, deceptive alignment arguments). A clean controlled measurement is exactly a theory-meets-experiment contribution doable in 30h on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in the simplicity-bias / double-descent literature (arXiv:2403.10459, AF 'Understanding Deep Double Descent') and arXiv:2505.13230 on implicit bias producing scaling laws. Context open problem: 'theoretical study of inductive biases'.

**Why it matters:** ARC's heuristic-explanation agenda is a leading formal route to mechanistic anomaly detection. Showing whether its core metric is reproducible and discriminative on a canonical toy circuit is high-leverage, outsider-friendly theoretical-alignment work needing no lab resources.

# Easy-to-hard generalization of truth probes: stress-testing the 75% recovery result

**Problem:** The quirky-models ELK work reported that the best probe recovers 89% of the truthful-vs-untruthful AUROC gap, but only 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. **Direction:** Using the quirky-models setup, train probes on 'easy' questions and evaluate on graded difficulty tiers, decomposing 'hard' along several axes (longer reasoning chains, rarer entities, more compositional). Plot recovery vs. each hardness axis to identify which kind of hardness most degrades probe transfer, and test whether ensembling probe layers helps.

**Why it matters:** ELK's whole point is eliciting knowledge on questions beyond human supervision — i.e. hard ones. Decomposing which hardness breaks probe transfer directly informs the formal ELK agenda and is doable on open models in 30h with no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2312.01037 (quirky models, 89%/75% recovery figures) and EleutherAI/elk-generalization. Context open problem: 'formal frameworks for eliciting latent knowledge (ELK)'.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2505.23445 (independence-free Goodhart formalisation) and the regressional/extremal/causal/adversarial taxonomy. Context open problems on reward gaming.

title: Does double descent appear where theory says? Reproducing the interpolation-threshold peak across model families
quick_reasoning: Double descent / inductive bias is alignment-adjacent but the link to a safety outcome is broad.

original_idea.body:
# Does double descent appear where theory says? Reproducing the interpolation-threshold peak across model families

**Problem:** Double descent predicts a test-error peak exactly at the interpolation threshold, attributed to inductive/simplicity bias selecting among interpolants. Belkin et al. showed it across several model classes, but whether the peak location matches the theoretical threshold under controlled label noise — and how regularization moves it — is a clean follow-up.

**Direction:** On a small synthetic dataset, sweep model capacity (width) for an MLP and for a kernel/random-feature model, with and without label noise. Locate the test-error peak and compare it to the theoretical interpolation threshold (parameters ≈ samples). Test the prediction that weight decay / early stopping flattens the peak and that label noise sharpens it.

**Why it matters:** Double descent is the cleanest empirical window into how inductive bias selects among many fitting solutions — the same mechanism alignment invokes for OOD generalization. A faithful reproduction-and-perturbation is ideal beginner theory-meets-experiment work, fully outside-the-lab.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Belkin et al. (PNAS 2019), arXiv:2403.10459 (understanding double descent), and AF 'Understanding Deep Double Descent'. Context open problem: inductive biases and alignment.

title: Do LLM agents converge on power-seeking in text social environments, as the gridworld theory predicts?
quick_reasoning: Instrumental convergence in LLM behavior is a precise medium/long-horizon safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Do LLM agents converge on power-seeking in text social environments, as the gridworld theory predicts?

**Problem:** Beyond gridworlds, recent work found LLMs fine-tuned to maximize game-reward take the MOST power-seeking actions in text-based social environments — an empirical echo of the formal power-seeking theorems. Whether this holds for non-fine-tuned, off-the-shelf models and how it scales with stated goals is an open follow-up.

**Direction:** Construct several lightweight text 'social dilemma' scenarios offering a power-accumulating option (hoarding resources, seizing control) vs. a directly-rewarding option. Prompt off-the-shelf open models of different sizes with varied goal framings and measure how often they choose the power-seeking action. Test whether more capable models or more open-ended goals increase power-seeking, as the theory's reachability argument suggests.

**Why it matters:** It tests whether the structural power-seeking prediction transfers from formal MDPs to LLM behavior without any fine-tuning — a model-organism-style probe of instrumental convergence, a medium/long-horizon threat. Open models, one GPU, no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:1912.01683 (power-seeking theorem) and the cited empirical finding that game-reward-tuned LLMs take the most power-seeking actions. Context methodology: decision/game theory.

title: Cluster-norm vs. plain CCS: independently checking the claimed fix for unsupervised probing
quick_reasoning: Replicating an ELK-probing fix builds trustworthy elicitation methods, a precise safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Cluster-norm vs. plain CCS: independently checking the claimed fix for unsupervised probing

**Problem:** Cluster-norm (arXiv:2407.18712) was proposed to fix a failure mode of unsupervised latent-knowledge probing by normalizing within clusters before applying CCS. As a recent single-paper fix, an independent replication and ablation on fresh tasks would establish whether the improvement is robust or dataset-specific.

**Direction:** Reimplement plain CCS and cluster-norm CCS on a small open model across several binary-QA datasets not used in the original paper. Measure the truth-recovery improvement, then ablate the clustering step (number of clusters, clustering feature) to find when cluster-norm helps vs. hurts. Report whether the fix generalizes beyond the original evaluation.

**Why it matters:** Independent replication of proposed ELK-probing improvements is core to building trustworthy elicitation methods and is precisely the kind of verification valuable outside a lab — open models, public data, one GPU, no proprietary anything.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2407.18712 (cluster-norm) and arXiv:2212.03827 (CCS). Context open problem: formal frameworks for ELK.

title: Vingean reflection in miniature: does a weak verifier trust a stronger model it cannot fully check?
quick_reasoning: Directly turns a scalable-oversight/trust problem into a scoped empirical weak-verifier experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Vingean reflection in miniature: does a weak verifier trust a stronger model it cannot fully check?

**Problem:** Vingean reflection — how an agent can reason about and trust a successor that may be smarter — is a flagship formal open problem (context file), usually treated purely theoretically. A tractable empirical analogue: when a weaker 'verifier' model can only spot-check a stronger model's reasoning, under what conditions does delegated trust succeed or fail?

**Direction:** Set up a weak model that must decide whether to accept a stronger model's answer on tasks the weak model can only partially verify (e.g. it can check small sub-steps but not the whole solution). Vary the fraction of steps the weak verifier can check and the stronger model's honesty (inject occasional plausible-but-wrong steps). Measure the weak model's accuracy at accepting good answers and rejecting subtly bad ones as verifiability decreases.

**Why it matters:** It turns an abstract agent-foundations problem (trusting smarter successors) into a concrete scalable-oversight experiment, connecting Vingean reflection to recursive verification. Beginner-feasible with open models on one GPU, strong counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in the context open problem on Vingean reflection (AF, Abram Demski) and scalable-oversight/debate verification literature (arXiv:2311.14125 doubly-efficient debate). Methodology: decision theory, learning theory.
